claim: Many types of adult stem cells exist in a state of cell-cycle quiescence.
source: Many types of adult stem cells exist in a state of cell-cycle quiescence, yet it has remained unclear whether quiescence plays a role in maintaining the stem cell fate.
evidence: This is a statement about the field presented in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Mitotically dividing germ cells—including germline stem cells—become quiescent in the absence of food.
source: We find that mitotically dividing germ cells—including germline stem cells—become quiescent in the absence of food.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented throughout the manuscript, including M-phase cell counts and cell-cycle analysis.

claim: Quiescence in C. elegans germ cells is characterized by a slowing of S phase.
source: This quiescence is characterized by a slowing of S phase, a block to M-phase entry, and the ability to re-enter M phase rapidly in response to re-feeding.
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling experiments showing slow progression through S phase during starvation (Figure 3).

claim: Quiescence in C. elegans germ cells is characterized by a block to M-phase entry.
source: This quiescence is characterized by a slowing of S phase, a block to M-phase entry, and the ability to re-enter M phase rapidly in response to re-feeding.
evidence: This is supported by the disappearance of M-phase cells during starvation (Figure 2).

claim: Quiescent germ cells can re-enter M phase rapidly in response to re-feeding.
source: This quiescence is characterized by a slowing of S phase, a block to M-phase entry, and the ability to re-enter M phase rapidly in response to re-feeding.
evidence: This is supported by the burst of M-phase cells observed 1-1.5 hours after re-feeding (Figure 2D, E).

claim: Cell-cycle quiescence alters the genetic requirements for stem cell maintenance.
source: Further, we demonstrate that cell-cycle quiescence alters the genetic requirements for stem cell maintenance: The signaling pathway required for stem cell maintenance under fed conditions—GLP-1/Notch signaling—becomes dispensable under conditions of quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by temperature-shift experiments with glp-1(q224ts) mutants showing stem cell maintenance during starvation without GLP-1/Notch signaling (Figure 6).

claim: GLP-1/Notch signaling is required for stem cell maintenance under fed conditions.
source: The signaling pathway required for stem cell maintenance under fed conditions—GLP-1/Notch signaling—becomes dispensable under conditions of quiescence.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript (Austin and Kimble, 1987) and confirmed in the current study.

claim: GLP-1/Notch signaling becomes dispensable for stem cell maintenance under conditions of quiescence.
source: The signaling pathway required for stem cell maintenance under fed conditions—GLP-1/Notch signaling—becomes dispensable under conditions of quiescence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that starved glp-1(q224ts) animals maintain germline stem cells at restrictive temperature (Figure 6).

claim: Cell-cycle quiescence can itself maintain stem cells, independent of the signaling pathway otherwise essential for such maintenance.
source: Thus, cell-cycle quiescence can itself maintain stem cells, independent of the signaling pathway otherwise essential for such maintenance.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results showing GLP-1/Notch independence during quiescence.

claim: The adult germline of C. elegans presents a tractable model for studying stem cell behavior because of its simple, linear organization.
source: The adult germline of C. elegans presents a tractable model for studying stem cell behavior because of its simple, linear organization (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a characterization of the model system supported by the schematic in Figure 1A.

claim: Mitotically dividing germ cells—including germline stem cells—reside in the distal region of the gonad (the 'progenitor zone').
source: Mitotically dividing germ cells—including germline stem cells—reside in the distal region of the gonad (the 'progenitor zone').
evidence: This is an established feature of C. elegans germline organization.

claim: Differentiating germ cells, in meiotic prophase, are located more proximally.
source: Differentiating germ cells, in meiotic prophase, are located more proximally.
evidence: This is an established feature of C. elegans germline organization.

claim: The progenitor zone is composed of a distal pool of germline stem cells and a more proximal pool of cells that have begun to differentiate.
source: The progenitor zone has been studied under fed conditions and is composed of a distal pool of germline stem cells and a more proximal pool of cells that have begun to differentiate (Cinquin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Under fed conditions, cells throughout the progenitor zone cycle asynchronously and continuously.
source: Under fed conditions, cells throughout the progenitor zone cycle asynchronously and continuously (Crittenden et al., 2006; Fox et al., 2011; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Morgan et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Transient progenitors undergo one or two rounds of division as they pass through the proximal progenitor zone.
source: with transient progenitors undergoing one or two rounds of division as they pass through the proximal progenitor zone (Fox and Schedl, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Food removal caused a drop in the number of M-phase cells in adult hermaphrodites.
source: Food removal caused a drop in the number of M-phase cells (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In hermaphrodites, the number of M-phase cells per progenitor zone dropped from an average of 7.6 before food removal to 2.1 after 30 min without food.
source: In hermaphrodites, the number of M-phase cells per progenitor zone dropped from an average of 7.6 before food removal to 2.1 after 30 min without food (n = 7 replicates of 220–551 gonadal arms per replicate per time point) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: After 3.5 hr without food, M-phase cells were virtually absent in hermaphrodites.
source: The number of M-phase cells continued to decline thereafter, and after 3.5 hr without food, M-phase cells were virtually absent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The drop in M-phase cells did not occur in hermaphrodites fed continuously.
source: This drop in M-phase cells did not occur in hermaphrodites fed continuously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, D)
evidence: This is a control experiment showing that the effect is specific to food removal.

claim: The drop in M-phase cells did not occur in hermaphrodites exposed to a mock starvation procedure.
source: nor in hermaphrodites exposed to a mock starvation procedure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a control experiment showing that the effect is specific to food removal.

claim: In males, M-phase cells also disappeared rapidly in response to food removal.
source: In males, M-phase cells also disappeared rapidly in response to food removal, although the initial drop in M-phase cells was not monotonically decreasing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In adults of both sexes, germ cells stop dividing quickly in the absence of food.
source: We conclude that in adults of both sexes, germ cells stop dividing quickly in the absence of food.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the M-phase cell counts in hermaphrodites and males.

claim: Re-feeding of starved hermaphrodites triggered a burst of M-phase cells 1.5 hr after the start of re-feeding.
source: In hermaphrodites, this treatment triggered a burst of M-phase cells 1.5 hr after the start of re-feeding (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Males showed a similar response to re-feeding, but the burst of M-phase cells occurred 1 hr earlier than in hermaphrodites.
source: Males showed a similar response to re-feeding, but the burst of M-phase cells occurred 1 hr earlier (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In both sexes, bursts of M-phase cells upon re-feeding included some individual germlines having approximately twice as many M-phase cells as were observed among continuously fed animals.
source: In both sexes, these bursts included some individual germlines having approximately twice as many M-phase cells as were observed among continuously fed animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: In both sexes, germ cells resume mitotic division rapidly in response to re-feeding.
source: These results demonstrate that in both sexes, germ cells resume mitotic division rapidly in response to re-feeding.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the re-feeding experiments showing rapid M-phase entry.

claim: The faster response to re-feeding in males is consistent with germ cells in males having a faster cell-cycle under continuously fed conditions.
source: The faster response in males is consistent with germ cells in males having a faster cell-cycle under continuously fed conditions (Morgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and prior work.

claim: The higher maxima of M-phase cells in re-fed versus continuously fed animals is consistent with germ cells collecting at the G2-to-M transition during starvation and entering M phase semi-synchronously upon re-feeding.
source: Further, the higher maxima of M-phase cells in re-fed versus continuously fed animals is consistent with germ cells collecting at the G2-to-M transition during starvation and entering M phase semi-synchronously upon re-feeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data.

claim: In starved L4 hermaphrodites, M-phase cells persisted for ~4–5 hr after food removal.
source: In starved L4s, M-phase cells persisted for ~4–5 hr after food removal, with the average number of M-phase cells only moderately reduced relative to fed animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The disappearance of M-phase cells in starved L4 hermaphrodites coincided with the molt into adulthood.
source: The disappearance of M-phase cells coincided with the molt into adulthood (~5–8 hr after food removal), and the coincidence of these events persisted even under conditions where the timing of this molt was changed
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and confirmed under different starvation conditions.

claim: Germ cells in hermaphrodites starved from L4 do not immediately stop dividing in response to food removal, but germ cell division eventually ceases, at or near the molt into adulthood.
source: These results demonstrate that germ cells in hermaphrodites starved from L4 do not immediately stop dividing in response to food removal, but germ cell division eventually ceases, at or near the molt into adulthood.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the timing of M-phase cell disappearance in L4-starved animals.

claim: Mitotically dividing germ cells in L4s are not equivalent to those in adults.
source: This finding suggests that mitotically dividing germ cells in L4s are not equivalent to those in adults, a result consistent with previous studies (Crittenden et al., 2002; Dalfo et al., 2012; Gerhold et al., 2015; Michaelson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the different responses to starvation and is consistent with prior work.

claim: The timing of M-phase entry upon re-feeding is largely unaffected by the duration of preceding starvation, at least during the first 72 hr of starvation.
source: We conclude that the timing of M-phase entry upon re-feeding is largely unaffected by the duration of preceding starvation, at least during the first 72 hr of starvation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from re-feeding experiments with different starvation durations (Figure 2F).

claim: The median cell-cycle length in fed early adult hermaphrodites is ~6.2 hr.
source: By labeling germlines with the thymidine analog 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) and monitoring the fraction of EdU+ M-phase cells over time, we estimated a median cell-cycle length in fed early adult hermaphrodites of ~6.2 hr
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: In fed early adult hermaphrodites, S phase lasts ~4.4 hr.
source: with S phase lasting ~4.4 hr
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: In fed early adult hermaphrodites, G2 lasts ~1.3 hr.
source: G2 lasting ~1.3 hr
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: In fed early adult hermaphrodites, G1 and M phase together last ~30 min.
source: and G1 and M phase together lasting ~30 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: For hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4, the median cell-cycle length is ~9.8 hr.
source: For this age group, we estimated a median cell-cycle length of ~9.8 hr
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: For hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4, median G1 length is <30 min.
source: with median G1, S-phase, and G2 lengths of <30 min
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: For hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4, median S-phase length is ~6.8 hr.
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: For hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4, median G2 length is ~2.3 hr.
source: and ~2.3 hr, respectively
evidence: This is a measurement from EdU labeling experiments.

claim: For hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4, there is a long-tailed distribution of G2 lengths.
source: but with a long-tailed distribution of G2 lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the EdU labeling experiments.

claim: During starvation, G1 cells disappeared following food removal, and the timing of their disappearance coincided with the disappearance of M-phase cells.
source: For all three age groups and for both sexes, G1 cells disappeared following food removal, and the timing of their disappearance coincided with the disappearance of M-phase cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During starvation, G1 cells continued to initiate S phase without a pronounced delay.
source: This result demonstrates that during starvation, G1 cells continued to initiate S phase without a pronounced delay.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that G1 cells disappear at the same rate as M-phase cells.

claim: During starvation, the fraction of S-phase cells decreased over time, and the fraction of G2 cells increased.
source: Our second observation was that for all age groups and sexes, the fraction of S-phase cells decreased over time during starvation, and the fraction of G2 cells increased (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S-phase and G2 fractions changed more slowly during starvation than expected from measurements of S-phase length in fed animals.
source: However, S-phase and G2 fractions changed more slowly during starvation than expected from measurements of S-phase length in fed animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the starvation time course to the fed cell-cycle measurements.

claim: During starvation, germ cells do not pause in G1 and instead continue through S phase and arrest in G2.
source: We conclude that during starvation, germ cells do not pause in G1 and instead continue through S phase and arrest in G2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell-cycle phase analysis during starvation.

claim: S-phase progression during starvation occurs much more slowly than under fed conditions.
source: However, S-phase progression occurs much more slowly than under fed conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the slow change in S-phase fractions during starvation.

claim: Two hours after re-feeding, 55% of cells, on average, had entered M phase in emb-30(tn377ts) hermaphrodites.
source: Two hours after re-feeding, 55% of cells, on average, had entered M phase (n = 60 gonadal arms)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the emb-30 re-feeding experiment.

claim: Four hours after re-feeding, 99% of cells had entered M phase in emb-30(tn377ts) hermaphrodites.
source: after 4 hr, this number reached 99% (n = 66 gonadal arms) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the emb-30 re-feeding experiment.

claim: Virtually all mitotically dividing germ cells completed the remainder of S phase and G2 within 4 hr of re-feeding.
source: Therefore, virtually all mitotically dividing germ cells completed the remainder of S phase and G2 within 4 hr of re-feeding
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the emb-30 re-feeding experiment.

claim: Re-feeding restores the rate of progression through S phase and earlier stages of G2.
source: Thus, not only does re-feeding trigger germ cells arrested in G2 to enter M phase, but re-feeding also restores the rate of progression through S phase and earlier stages of G2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the emb-30 re-feeding experiment showing rapid completion of S phase and G2.

claim: Germ cells in glp-1(oz112gf) germline tumors responded normally to starvation and re-feeding.
source: Germ cells in both genotypes of germline tumors responded normally to starvation and re-feeding: Outside the region normally corresponding to the progenitor zone (i.e. outside the distal-most 20 rows of germ cells), M-phase cells disappeared quickly in response to food removal and re-bounded 1 to 2 hr after re-feeding (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Germ cells in gld-3(q730) nos-3(q650) germline tumors responded normally to starvation and re-feeding.
source: Germ cells in both genotypes of germline tumors responded normally to starvation and re-feeding: Outside the region normally corresponding to the progenitor zone (i.e. outside the distal-most 20 rows of germ cells), M-phase cells disappeared quickly in response to food removal and re-bounded 1 to 2 hr after re-feeding (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Proximity to the distal tip cell—the germline stem cell niche—is not required for a normal starvation and re-feeding response.
source: These results demonstrate that proximity to the distal tip cell—the germline stem cell niche—is not required for a normal starvation and re-feeding response.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the germline tumor experiments.

claim: Constitutive GLP-1/Notch signaling or combined loss of gld-3 and nos-3 does not promote germ cell proliferation per se, but rather promotes an undifferentiated fate in which cells divide only in the presence of food.
source: Additionally, these results refine our understanding of the control of germ cell fate: Constitutive GLP-1/Notch signaling or combined loss of gld-3 and nos-3 does not promote germ cell proliferation per se, but rather promotes an undifferentiated fate in which cells divide only in the presence of food.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that germline tumor cells still respond to starvation by ceasing division.

claim: Under fed conditions, maintenance of germline stem cells requires GLP-1/Notch signaling.
source: Under fed conditions, maintenance of these stem cells requires GLP-1/Notch signaling (Austin and Kimble, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In fed animals, removal of GLP-1/Notch signaling causes germline stem cells to be lost.
source: In fed animals, removal of GLP-1/Notch signaling causes germline stem cells to be lost: Germline stem cells fail to self-renew, and instead all germ cells enter the meiotic cell cycle (Austin and Kimble, 1987; Cinquin et al., 2010; Fox and Schedl, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: In fed glp-1(q224ts) controls, incubation at the restrictive temperature caused all germ cells to enter the meiotic cell cycle.
source: In fed controls, incubation at the restrictive temperature caused all germ cells to enter the meiotic cell cycle: Chromosomes adopted the 'crescent' shape (Figure 6A), and GLD-1 levels in the distal-most germ cells rose (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6I.

claim: In starved glp-1(q224ts) animals, meiotic entry did not occur at the restrictive temperature.
source: In starved animals, by contrast, meiotic entry did not occur: 99% (n = 214) of progenitor zones retained germ cells with a interphase chromosome morphology (Figure 6C), and GLD-1 levels in the distal-most germ cells remained low (n = 47 of 47 gonadal arms) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6I.

claim: Germ cells in starved glp-1(q224ts) animals retained the capacity for mitotic cell division.
source: Importantly, germ cells in starved animals retained the capacity for mitotic cell division, because when starved animals were re-fed at the restrictive temperature, their germ cells re-entered M phase (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Germ cells in starved glp-1(q224ts) animals retained the capacity for long-term self-renewal.
source: Germ cells in starved animals also retained the capacity for long-term self-renewal, because when starved animals were instead returned to the permissive temperature and re-fed for 2–3 days, 91% (n = 148) of progenitor zones retained germ cells in the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Starved animals maintain germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch.
source: These results demonstrate that starved animals maintain germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the glp-1(q224ts) temperature-shift experiments.

claim: Starvation inhibits the meiotic entry of germline stem cells, even in the absence of GLP-1/Notch.
source: In other words, starvation inhibits the meiotic entry of germline stem cells, even in the absence of GLP-1/Notch.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the glp-1(q224ts) temperature-shift experiments.

claim: The inhibition of meiotic entry during starvation was reversible upon re-feeding.
source: Similar to cell-cycle quiescence, this inhibition of meiotic entry was reversible upon re-feeding, because when starved glp-1(q224ts) animals were re-fed at the restrictive temperature, all germ cells eventually entered the meiotic cell cycle (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: High NaCl permitted maintenance of germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch in 48–79% of gonadal arms.
source: For both high NaCl and absence of sperm, 48–79% (n = 129–231) of gonadal arms retained germ cells in the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Absence of sperm permitted maintenance of germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch in 48–79% of gonadal arms.
source: For both high NaCl and absence of sperm, 48–79% (n = 129–231) of gonadal arms retained germ cells in the mitotic cell cycle (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Three stress conditions that inhibit or reduce germ cell division (starvation, high NaCl, and absence of sperm) also permitted maintenance of germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch.
source: Thus, three stress conditions that inhibit or reduce germ cell division (starvation, high NaCl, and absence of sperm) also permitted maintenance of germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from multiple conditions.

claim: Cell-cycle quiescence itself is an effector of stem cell maintenance.
source: This commonality suggests that cell-cycle quiescence itself is an effector of stem cell maintenance (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the commonality across different quiescence-inducing conditions.

claim: Stem cell maintenance in the absence of GLP-1/Notch was not permitted by cell-cycle arrest caused by RNAi knockdown of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (cdk-1).
source: Nonetheless, such maintenance is not simply a function of inhibiting passage through M-phase, because stem cell maintenance in the absence of GLP-1/Notch was not permitted by cell-cycle arrest caused by RNAi knockdown of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (cdk-1) (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Starvation inhibits the meiotic entry of transient progenitors.
source: We conclude that starvation slows or blocks the meiotic entry of transient progenitors, similar to its effect on the meiotic entry of germline stem cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the emb-30 experiments comparing re-feeding to continued starvation.

claim: Starvation-induced quiescence is distinct from cell-cycle arrest caused by DNA damage.
source: Following three criteria, starvation-induced quiescence was distinct from cell-cycle arrest caused by DNA damage.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing multiple features of starvation-induced quiescence to DNA damage-induced arrest.

claim: DNA damage strongly up-regulates inhibitory phosphorylation of CDK-1.
source: First, DNA damage strongly up-regulates inhibitory phosphorylation of CDK-1 (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Craig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and supported by prior work.

claim: Starvation-induced quiescence did not up-regulate inhibitory phosphorylation of CDK-1.
source: By contrast, starvation-induced quiescence did not up-regulate this phosphorylation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: DNA damage causes germ cell nuclei to enlarge.
source: Second, DNA damage causes germ cell nuclei to enlarge (Figure 7A; Gartner et al., 2000)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and supported by prior work.

claim: Starvation-induced quiescence did not cause nuclei to enlarge.
source: By contrast, starvation-induced quiescence did not cause nuclei to enlarge (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cell-cycle arrest in response to DNA damage requires the p53 homolog cep-1.
source: Third, cell-cycle arrest in response to DNA damage requires the p53 homolog cep-1 (Derry et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Starvation-induced quiescence did not require cep-1.
source: By contrast, starvation-induced quiescence did not require cep-1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Starvation and DNA damage induce cell-cycle arrest differently.
source: We conclude that starvation and DNA damage induce cell-cycle arrest differently.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the multiple differences between starvation-induced quiescence and DNA damage-induced arrest.

claim: Mutations in the TGF-β pathway, insulin/IGF-1 pathway, or AMPK pathway are not individually required for starvation-induced quiescence in adult germ cells.
source: We conclude that each of the genes tested is not individually required for starvation-induced quiescence in adult germ cells
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that M-phase cells disappeared quickly in all tested mutants (Figure 7B).

claim: Quiescence in adult germ cells is not affected by exogenous serotonin.
source: likewise, quiescence is not affected by exogenous serotonin.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Quiescence in adults is controlled differently than cell-cycle responses in the larval germline.
source: These findings suggest that quiescence in adults is controlled differently than cell-cycle responses in the larval germline and is largely independent of behavioral responses to food.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of requirement for factors affecting larval responses.

claim: Quiescence in adult germ cells is largely independent of behavioral responses to food.
source: These findings suggest that quiescence in adults is controlled differently than cell-cycle responses in the larval germline and is largely independent of behavioral responses to food.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of factors affecting behavioral responses.

claim: In the absence of food, adult germ cells in C. elegans stop dividing and become quiescent.
source: Briefly, we find that in the absence of food, adult germ cells in C. elegans stop dividing and become quiescent (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Quiescence in C. elegans germ cells is characterized by a slowing of S phase and a block to M-phase entry, such that cells arrest in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
source: This quiescence is characterized by a slowing of S phase and a block to M-phase entry, such that cells arrest in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Quiescence maintains germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch, a signal required for stem cell maintenance under conditions of active proliferation.
source: Further, this quiescence maintains germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch, a signal required for stem cell maintenance under conditions of active proliferation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Re-feeding causes germ cells to exit quiescence rapidly.
source: Re-feeding causes germ cells to exit quiescence rapidly, and a requirement for GLP-1/Notch signaling similarly resumes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A requirement for GLP-1/Notch signaling resumes upon re-feeding.
source: Re-feeding causes germ cells to exit quiescence rapidly, and a requirement for GLP-1/Notch signaling similarly resumes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Adult stem cells were once thought to exist primarily in a state of cell-cycle quiescence.
source: Stem cells in adult tissues were once thought to exist primarily in a state of cell-cycle quiescence.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical view in the field.

claim: Quiescence was viewed as an inherent property of the stem cell fate and thus essential for a tissue's long-term self-renewal.
source: Such quiescence was viewed as an inherent property of the stem cell fate and thus essential for a tissue's long-term self-renewal (Hall and Watt, 1989; Potten and Loeffler, 1990).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Adult stem cells are not universally quiescent but instead cycle in accordance with the needs of the tissue.
source: More recently, however, it has become clear that adult stem cells are not universally quiescent but instead cycle in accordance with the needs of the tissue: Some types of stem cells proliferate continuously, whereas others switch from quiescence to rapid proliferation in response to certain stimuli (e.g. wounding or hormones) (Wabik and Jones, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about current understanding in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Hematopoietic and neural stem cells reversibly switch between quiescence and active proliferation in response to tissue injury.
source: In mammals, for example, hematopoietic and neural stem cells reversibly switch between quiescence and active proliferation in response to tissue injury (Doetsch et al., 1999; Harrison and Lerner, 1991; Lugert et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mammary stem cells expand transiently during pregnancy and the estrus cycle.
source: and mammary stem cells expand transiently during pregnancy and the estrus cycle (Asselin-Labat et al., 2010; Joshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic or environmental perturbations that impact the cell cycle can also affect stemness.
source: Nevertheless, genetic or environmental perturbations that impact the cell cycle can also affect stemness (Orford and Scadden, 2008; Pietras et al., 2011; Yilmaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The progenitor zone in C. elegans has been studied under fed conditions.
source: The progenitor zone has been studied under fed conditions
evidence: This is a statement about prior work on the C. elegans germline.

claim: Prior to this work, germ cell proliferation in C. elegans adults had not been examined in detail under food-limited conditions.
source: Prior to this work, germ cell proliferation in C. elegans adults had not been examined in detail under food-limited conditions.

claim: In Drosophila, nutrient limitation or changes in nutrient-sensing pathways slow germ cell proliferation, reduce germline stem cell number, or both.
